title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction
abstract: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra $\mathbb{F}_2[\mathbb{Z}_\ell]$, which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as $[[169,13,11]]$, $[[143,15,9]]$, and $[[260,24,10]]$, including a $[[247,19,14]]$ code that achieves the highest ${kd^2}/{n}$ among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.
summary: This paper introduces LiftDiff, a novel generative framework that uses discrete denoising diffusion models to discover high-performing Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs). By training the model to generate base matrices guided by quantum code properties, the authors efficiently search the vast code space, yielding codes that outperform existing benchmarks in terms of error correction capability.
main_problem: The primary challenge is discovering Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs) that achieve a high encoding rate while maintaining sufficient error-correcting distance.
main_result: The proposed LiftDiff method successfully discovers novel QECCs, such as [[247, 19, 14]], that outperform established codes like the Gross code across various noise models.
method: The authors introduce LiftDiff, a generative framework that uses a discrete denoising diffusion model trained on base matrices to construct Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) quantum codes.
model_or_system: The system involves constructing QECCs, specifically Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, by generating their base matrices over the group algebra F2[Z_l]. The process is guided by an energy function that incorporates code properties.
key_observables: Code parameters like $[[n, k, d]]$, girth, degree, sparsity, and the Logical Error Rate (LER) under physical error rates ($p$).
important_parameters: The physical error rate $p$ (tested from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-4}$), and the code parameters themselves (e.g., $[[260, 24, 10]]$).
main_assumptions: The guidance mechanism relies on the differentiability of quantum code properties (like girth and decoding error) to steer the diffusion sampler.
figures_summary: Figure 4 compares the Logical Error Rate (LER) vs. physical error rate ($p$) for codes generated by LiftDiff against a baseline code, showing superior performance for the generated codes. Other figures illustrate the effect of the guidance mechanism on code structure.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of QECC design, details the LiftDiff methodology (training the diffusion model on base matrices and using a guided reverse process), presents the energy function incorporating multiple code diagnostics, and concludes with performance comparisons showing the efficacy of the generative approach.
why_interesting: The application of advanced generative AI models, like diffusion processes, to the highly structured and mathematically complex domain of quantum error correction is a significant methodological advance for quantum information theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the inference process. The matrix Mt and timestep t are input to the model, producing logits zt. The logits are passed through a sigmoid function and fed into the guidance mechanism, whose output adjusts the prediction to obtain zg t . The guided logits are passed through a second sigmoid function, and the resulting output is used to produce Mt−1.

Figure 2: Selected codes from Table 1 against the baselines. Each marker is one code, colored by its wchk. Circles are codes from this work, tagged with their row number in Table 1. Squares are BB codes of Bravyi et al. (2024) and diamonds the CSS codes of Cruz-Benito et al. (2026). (a) Encoding rate k/n against distance d. (b) Block length n against kd2/n.
